questions.question: What is the main practical benefit of `StyleSheet.create` over an inline style object?
options: It adds CSS selectors and cascading to React Native
It validates style shapes during development and lets styles be referenced by a lightweight ID instead of resending the full object every render
It is required for Flexbox to work at all
It converts styles into real CSS files at build time
questions.explanation: StyleSheet.create doesn't change what the styles do — it's a development-time validation and a small performance optimization over passing fresh inline objects.

questions.question: What is React Native's default `flexDirection`, and how does it differ from the web?
options: row, same as the web's flexbox default
column — the opposite of the web's row default for flex containers
React Native has no default flex direction
It depends on the platform (iOS vs Android)
questions.explanation: Every View is a flex container by default, and that default direction is column, which surprises developers coming from web CSS where flex-direction: row is the default.

questions.question: What layout systems besides Flexbox are available in React Native?
options: None — Flexbox is the only layout system; there is no Grid, float, or display: block
questions.explanation: Unlike the web, which has multiple layout modes, React Native layout is Flexbox-only (though individual elements can still opt into position: 'absolute').

questions.question: What does a unitless number like `width: 200` represent in a React Native style?
options: 200 CSS pixels, exactly as on the web
200 density-independent points, which the platform scales for the device's screen density
It's invalid — all dimensions require an explicit unit string
questions.explanation: React Native has no px/em/rem units; plain numbers are density-independent points scaled appropriately per device, which is why percentages are written as strings like "50%" but fixed sizes are plain numbers.
